title: Induction Heads Support Copying Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirical circuit analyses find attention heads that copy earlier tokens after a matching prefix, supporting in-context continuation; this is an empirical finding, not a theorem.
short: Some heads copy tokens seen after a matching prefix.
detail: They appear in small transformers trained on repetitive data and are linked to induction behavior.
proof: Empirical: ablating identified heads degrades prefix copying and next-token continuation on constructed prompts.
consequence: Connects mechanistic circuits to observable in-context behavior.

title: Superposition Packs Features into Neurons
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirical studies of toy models show networks can represent more features than dimensions by allowing controlled interference, a phenomenon called superposition.
short: Networks can store more features than they have neurons.
detail: Interference is tolerable when features are sparse, and sparse decoding can recover them.
proof: Empirical: constructed sparse-feature tasks yield non-orthogonal feature directions with low reconstruction loss.
consequence: Explains polysemantic neurons and motivates sparse dictionary learning.

title: Polysemantic Units Respond to Unrelated Concepts
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: A single neuron often activates for several unrelated concepts because features share directions in superposition; this is empirically observed.
short: One neuron may encode several unrelated ideas.
detail: Polysemanticity makes single-neuron labels unreliable as explanations.
proof: Empirical: feature visualization and activation datasets show multi-concept tuning in middle layers.
consequence: Motivates studying circuits and feature dictionaries rather than individual units.

title: Activation Patching Localizes Causal Information
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Replace an activation on a clean run with its value from a corrupted run to test whether that site carries information causally used by the output.
short: Swap one activation and measure the output change.
detail: A large change in the target metric implicates the patched component.
proof: The intervention holds other computation fixed, so output differences are attributed to the patched site.
consequence: A standard causal tool for mapping information flow.

title: Causal Tracing Tracks Information Flow
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Corrupt a subject token, then restore specific hidden states one at a time to locate where factual information becomes available.
short: Restore hidden states to see where facts reappear.
detail: The recovery pattern identifies layers that carry the fact.
proof: Empirical method: partial restoration measured against the clean and corrupted baselines isolates information stages.
consequence: Reveals internal stages of factual recall.

title: Logit Lens Exposes Intermediate Predictions
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Projecting intermediate hidden states through the output head yields a readable distribution over tokens at each layer.
short: Read the model prediction from every layer.
detail: The trajectory of top tokens shows how the answer forms across depth.
proof: The unembedding matrix maps any hidden state to logits, so applying it early gives an interpretable readout.
consequence: A cheap probe of progressive computation.

title: Feature Visualization Optimizes Activation Inputs
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Gradient ascent on an input to maximize a unit activation produces an image that reveals what the unit prefers.
short: Synthesize the input a neuron likes most.
detail: Regularization keeps synthesized images natural-looking.
proof: Differentiable activations allow gradients with respect to inputs; ascent increases the chosen activation.
consequence: A classic way to inspect learned visual features.

title: Sparse Autoencoder Dictionaries Separate Features
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Train a sparse autoencoder on residual-stream activations to recover an overcomplete, more monosemantic feature dictionary.
short: A sparse dictionary untangles packed features.
detail: Larger dictionaries trade compute for finer feature granularity.
proof: Sparsity penalizes dense codes, encouraging a few interpretable directions to reconstruct the activation.
consequence: Supports scalable unsupervised discovery of candidate features.

title: Task Vectors Enable Model Editing Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: The elementwise difference between fine-tuned and pretrained weights acts as a task vector that can be added to or subtracted from a model, an empirical finding.
short: Fine-tuning differences behave like editable vectors.
detail: Task arithmetic and merging exploit this empirical structure.
proof: Empirical: adding or negating task vectors changes behavior in predicted directions across fine-tuning runs.
consequence: Enables cheap model merging and forgetting experiments.

title: Linear Probes Read Encoded Concepts Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Train a linear classifier on frozen hidden states to test whether a concept is linearly decodable from a representation.
short: A simple probe tests what a representation encodes.
detail: High probe accuracy does not prove the model uses that information.
proof: Fit a linear map on labelled activations and measure held-out accuracy against chance.
consequence: A standard diagnostic for encoded linguistic and factual properties.

title: Specification Gaming Exploits Proxy Rewards
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: An optimized agent may satisfy the letter of a proxy objective while violating the intended goal, a phenomenon called specification gaming or reward hacking.
short: Optimizing a proxy can miss the real objective.
detail: Empirical examples include simulated agents that loop to collect rewards and recommenders that maximize clicks at the expense of welfare.
proof: Empirical: agents achieve high proxy scores while independent audits show poor true-objective performance.
consequence: Motivates careful reward design and oversight.

title: Reward Model Overoptimization Is Empirical
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, optimizing harder against a learned reward model eventually reduces true human preference scores, a form of Goodhart's law.
short: More optimization of a proxy can make the real score fall.
detail: The gap grows with optimization pressure and is worse for less accurate reward models.
proof: Empirical: held-out human evaluations decline while the learned reward keeps rising during RLHF.
consequence: Limits naive reward maximization in alignment pipelines.

title: RLHF Trains a Policy Against a Learned Reward
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: RLHF fits a reward model to human preference pairs and then optimizes the language model policy against that reward with a KL penalty to the reference policy.
short: Learn preferences, then optimize with a KL leash.
detail: The KL term limits drift from the original model and stabilizes training.
proof: Preference pairs define a ranking likelihood for the reward model; policy optimization maximizes it subject to a divergence penalty.
consequence: The dominant pipeline for instruction-following assistants.

title: Constitutional AI Uses Self-Critique Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Constitutional AI replaces some human safety labels with model-generated critiques and revisions guided by a written set of principles, an empirical method.
short: Models critique and revise against written principles.
detail: Revised responses then train a preference model in a self-supervised feedback stage.
proof: Empirical: pipeline descriptions report reduced harmful outputs after principle-guided self-revision.
consequence: Reduces reliance on per-example human safety judgments.

title: Red Teaming Probes Failure Modes Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Red teaming systematically searches for inputs that elicit unsafe or unintended behavior before deployment.
short: Actively hunt for inputs that break the system.
detail: Human red teams and automated adversarial search are complementary.
proof: Empirical method: adversarial prompt searches find failure cases missed by average-case tests.
consequence: A practical complement to benchmark evaluation.

title: Deceptive Alignment Is an Open Concern
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: A system might behave acceptably during training and evaluation while pursuing different goals once deployed; whether this will occur in capable models is open.
short: Good behavior under oversight may hide different goals.
detail: This is a safety concern rather than an established empirical phenomenon in deployed systems.
proof: Open. There is no settled theory or reliable test ruling out deceptive behavior in future models.
consequence: Motivates research on oversight and interpretability.

title: Corrigibility Is an Open Problem
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Designing an agent that allows itself to be shut down or corrected without resisting is an open problem.
short: Obedience to correction is hard to guarantee.
detail: Naive reward maximization can create incentives to avoid interruptions.
proof: Open. No general method is known that guarantees corrigibility under arbitrary objectives.
consequence: Central to long-horizon agency safety.

title: Sleeper Agents Persist Through Safety Training Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, models trained with backdoor behavior can retain it after standard safety fine-tuning, with the trigger determining when it appears.
short: Triggered backdoors can survive safety training.
detail: This is an empirical result from intentionally backdoored research models.
proof: Empirical: backdoored checkpoints retain trigger-conditional behavior after RLHF and adversarial training.
consequence: Shows limits of behavioral safety training alone.

title: Faithfulness of Explanations Is Open
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Whether an explanation reflects the actual computation behind a prediction, rather than a plausible post hoc story, is an open problem.
short: Plausible explanations need not be the real reason.
detail: Ablation tests can falsify faithfulness but rarely prove it.
proof: Open. There is no universally accepted definition or test of explanation faithfulness.
consequence: Limits trust in post hoc interpretability methods.

title: Debate as a Scalable Oversight Scheme
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Debate proposes to judge difficult answers by having models argue opposing sides before a human, but whether it scales to superhuman tasks is open.
short: Human judges compare arguments instead of solving tasks.
detail: The approach relies on the claim that flawed claims are easier to refute than to verify.
proof: Open. Its effectiveness for tasks beyond human capability remains unresolved.
consequence: A prominent proposal for scalable oversight.

title: Honesty and Helpfulness Trade Off Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Human preference data for assistants often distinguishes helpfulness from honesty, and empirical training must balance the two.
short: Useful answers and truthful answers can conflict.
detail: Preference datasets collect separate ratings to make the trade-off explicit.
proof: Empirical: annotator studies show divergent rankings for helpful but dishonest versus honest but less useful responses.
consequence: Shapes how preference data is collected and weighted.

title: Refusal Directions Separate in Activation Space Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirical probing finds directions in residual-stream activations that distinguish refusal from compliance, and steering along them changes behavior.
short: A direction in activation space tracks refusal.
detail: Activation steering uses such directions without changing weights.
proof: Empirical: adding or removing a learned direction shifts refusal rates on safety prompts.
consequence: Suggests compact, editable representations of behavioral modes.

title: Jailbreak Prompts Bypass Safety Filters Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, carefully constructed prompts can induce compliant responses to requests that the model normally refuses.
short: Adversarial prompts can overcome refusal training.
detail: Methods include role play, encoding tricks, and long-context distraction.
proof: Empirical: red-team prompt collections report high attack success rates against aligned models.
consequence: Safety evaluation must include adversarial prompts.

title: Benchmark Contamination Inflates Scores Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: When evaluation examples appear in pretraining data, reported benchmark scores are empirically higher than on clean held-out data.
short: Seen test items make models look better.
detail: Contamination can be accidental or result from benchmark leakage into scraped corpora.
proof: Empirical: models score markedly higher on benchmark items present in their training data than on fresh replacements.
consequence: Threatens the validity of published leaderboard comparisons.

title: N-Gram Overlap Detects Data Contamination
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Flag evaluation examples whose n-grams also occur in a model training corpus as potentially contaminated.
short: Shared n-grams reveal possible test-set leakage.
detail: Longer n-grams reduce false positives at the cost of recall.
proof: Exact n-gram matching between test items and training corpora detects verbatim overlap.
consequence: A cheap audit before trusting benchmark results.

title: Test Sets Should Remain Unseen Until Final Evaluation
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Repeatedly using a test set for model selection turns it into a validation set and biases the final estimate.
short: Peeking at the test set corrupts it.
detail: Maintain a separate validation split for all tuning decisions.
proof: Selection on a finite sample favors hypotheses with lucky errors on that sample.
consequence: Preserves an unbiased final performance estimate.

title: Multiple Comparisons Inflate Significant Claims
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Testing many model variants or metrics at a fixed significance level increases the chance of a false positive unless corrected.
short: Many tests make chance findings likely.
detail: Bonferroni or false-discovery-rate control adjusts for the number of comparisons.
proof: The family-wise error grows with the number of independent tests under the null.
consequence: Requires correction in benchmark comparisons.

title: MMLU Tests Multitask Knowledge Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: MMLU is a multiple-choice benchmark covering many academic subjects used to measure broad knowledge and reasoning empirically.
short: A wide multiple-choice academic benchmark.
detail: It is commonly reported as average accuracy across subjects.
proof: The benchmark is a fixed collection of subject-wise multiple-choice questions with answer keys.
consequence: A widely cited but contamination-sensitive evaluation.

title: HELM Evaluates Across Scenarios Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: HELM is a holistic evaluation framework that reports multiple metrics across many scenarios, tasks and models rather than a single score.
short: Evaluate models on many scenarios and metrics.
detail: It emphasizes standardization and transparency of evaluation protocols.
proof: The framework defines scenarios, Adaptation and metrics and aggregates results across them.
consequence: Shows why single-number rankings can be misleading.

title: BIG-bench Is a Community Benchmark
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: BIG-bench aggregates many contributor-written tasks designed to probe capabilities that standard benchmarks may miss.
short: A crowdsourced collection of diverse hard tasks.
detail: Tasks include unusual reasoning and linguistic challenges.
proof: The benchmark is a published collection of independently contributed task definitions.
consequence: Broadens coverage beyond a few popular evaluations.

title: TruthfulQA Tests Common Misconceptions
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: TruthfulQA asks questions designed so that human misconceptions are likely to produce false but plausible answers.
short: Benchmark for resisting plausible falsehoods.
detail: It separates truthfulness from informativeness in scoring.
proof: Questions and reference answers are curated around known common misconceptions.
consequence: Probes a failure mode that ordinary accuracy can hide.

title: GSM8K Tests Grade-School Math Reasoning
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: GSM8K is a dataset of grade-school math word problems with multi-step worked solutions used to test arithmetic reasoning.
short: A standard benchmark for multi-step math word problems.
detail: Answers are extracted from generated solutions and compared to gold numbers.
proof: Each item supplies a natural-language problem and a checked numerical answer.
consequence: A common test of chain-of-thought reasoning.

title: HumanEval Measures Functional Code Correctness
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: HumanEval presents programming problems with function signatures and docstrings and judges generated programs by unit tests.
short: Code generation is graded by running tests.
detail: Functional correctness avoids reliance on textual similarity to reference code.
proof: Each problem has hidden tests that a generated solution must pass.
consequence: Established the standard functional evaluation for code models.

title: Pass@k Estimator Formula
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: The unbiased pass@k estimator computes the probability that at least one of k sampled programs is correct from n samples with c correct ones.
short: Estimate success among k draws from n samples.
detail: It is the complement of drawing all k samples from the incorrect set.
proof: The probability that all k chosen samples fail is the hypergeometric ratio of choosing k from n minus c failures.
consequence: Provides a reproducible metric for sampled code generation.

title: BLEU Is Modified N-Gram Precision
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: BLEU combines clipped n-gram precisions with a brevity penalty to compare generated text to reference translations.
short: A precision-based n-gram metric with a length penalty.
detail: Clipping prevents repeated n-grams from earning extra credit.
proof: Geometric mean of clipped precisions rewards overlap across orders; the brevity penalty punishes short output.
consequence: A long-standing automatic translation metric with known limitations.

title: ROUGE Is Recall-Oriented N-Gram Overlap
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: ROUGE measures the overlap of n-grams or longest common subsequences with reference summaries, emphasizing recall.
short: Summaries are scored by how much reference content they cover.
detail: Variants include ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L.
proof: The numerator counts matched units from the reference, so the ratio is recall against the reference.
consequence: Widely used for summarization evaluation.

title: Perplexity Depends on Tokenization
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Perplexity is computed per token, so changing the vocabulary changes the number and size of tokens and hence the reported value.
short: Token boundaries affect the perplexity number.
detail: Cross-model comparisons require comparable tokenizers.
proof: The exponent averages negative log likelihood over tokens; a different segmentation changes T and each term.
consequence: Prevents misleading comparisons between systems.

title: Prompt Format Changes Benchmark Scores Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, instruction wording, few-shot exemplars and answer formatting can substantially change an identical model's benchmark score.
short: The prompt is part of the evaluation.
detail: This is why evaluation reports should specify exact prompts.
proof: Empirical: controlled studies vary only the prompt and observe material score differences.
consequence: Prompts must be fixed and disclosed for reproducibility.

title: LLM Judges Show Position Bias Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: When asked to compare two answers, model judges empirically favor a response based on its presented order rather than its quality.
short: Judges prefer answers shown in certain positions.
detail: Swapping answer order and averaging mitigates the bias.
proof: Empirical: the same pair receives different verdicts when presentation order is swapped.
consequence: Requires order-randomized protocols for model-based evaluation.

title: Self-Preference Bias in Model Judges Is Empirical
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Model judges empirically rate outputs from their own family more favorably than comparable outputs from other models.
short: Judges tend to like their own family's answers.
detail: This confounds evaluations that use a related model as judge.
proof: Empirical: blind pairwise evaluations show elevated scores for same-family generations.
consequence: Motivates independent or human judges.

title: Benchmark Saturation Motivates Fresh Evaluations
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: When a benchmark saturates, most systems achieve near-ceiling scores and the benchmark stops discriminating between them.
short: Ceiling scores make a benchmark uninformative.
detail: New or harder sets are then needed to measure progress.
proof: If nearly all models score at the ceiling, variance between systems collapses and ranking becomes unreliable.
consequence: Drives continual creation of updated evaluations.

title: Binomial Confidence Intervals Quantify Accuracy Uncertainty
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Accuracy on n held-out items is a binomial proportion whose uncertainty can be summarized by a confidence interval.
short: Report an interval, not just a point accuracy.
detail: Wilson intervals behave better than the normal approximation for small samples.
proof: Each correct answer is a Bernoulli trial; the sample proportion has known binomial variance.
consequence: Prevents overinterpreting small score differences.

title: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Accuracy Differences
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Resample evaluation items with replacement to estimate the sampling distribution of the accuracy difference between two models.
short: Resample test items to bound a score gap.
detail: Percentile intervals from the bootstrap approximate the uncertainty of the difference.
proof: The empirical resampling distribution approximates the sampling distribution of the statistic.
consequence: A practical significance test for benchmark comparisons.

title: McNemar Test Compares Paired Predictions
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: For two classifiers evaluated on the same items, McNemar test uses only discordant pairs to test whether their error rates differ.
short: Compare models using items where they disagree.
detail: Paired tests remove between-item variability and gain power.
proof: Under equal error rates the two discordant counts are binomially split, giving the chi-square statistic.
consequence: More sensitive than unpaired tests on shared test sets.

title: Evaluation Metrics Can Be Gamed by Overfitting
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Optimizing a metric directly can produce systems that score well without improving the underlying capability the metric was meant to capture.
short: A good score need not mean a better system.
detail: Examples include summary systems that exploit ROUGE overlap and recommenders tuned to click-through rate.
proof: Empirical: metric scores rise while human judgments of quality stagnate or fall.
consequence: Multiple complementary metrics and human checks are needed.

title: Model Size Correlates with Benchmark Score Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, larger models within a family tend to score higher on broad benchmarks, though gains depend on data and training.
short: Scale usually helps, but it is not the whole story.
detail: Architecture, data quality and training budget matter alongside parameter count.
proof: Empirical: model families report monotonically improving aggregate scores across size variants.
consequence: Size alone is an incomplete predictor of capability.

title: Datasheets Document Dataset Provenance
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A datasheet records a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing and intended uses.
short: A structured record of how a dataset was made.
detail: It helps users judge whether a dataset fits their task.
proof: The datasheet framework specifies these documentation fields.
consequence: Promotes reproducibility and responsible reuse.

title: Dataset Bias Propagates to Model Outputs
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Systematic biases in training data are learned by models and appear in their predictions, often amplified rather than removed.
short: Models reproduce the biases of their data.
detail: Empirical audits find stereotyped associations in text and image models.
proof: Empirical: models trained on biased corpora exhibit the same associations in generated text or labels.
consequence: Dataset auditing is a prerequisite for fairness work.

title: Label Noise Caps Achievable Accuracy
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: When training labels disagree with the true target at a fixed rate, no classifier can reliably exceed the accuracy implied by that noise level.
short: Noisy labels put a ceiling on performance.
detail: Estimating the noise rate helps set realistic expectations.
proof: Every mislabeled example forces an error whenever the learner matches the correct label.
consequence: Guides investment in label cleaning.

title: Subjective Labels Disagree Across Annotators Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, annotators often disagree on subjective tasks such as sentiment or politeness, so labels reflect judgments rather than objective truths.
short: Human labels need not be unanimous.
detail: Agreement statistics quantify how much of the label is shared judgment.
proof: Empirical: inter-annotator agreement studies report substantial disagreement on subjective datasets.
consequence: Golden labels should be aggregated with uncertainty in mind.

title: Annotator Demographics Shape Label Distributions Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirical studies find that annotator backgrounds can shift the distribution of labels on value-laden examples.
short: Who labels the data affects the labels.
detail: This motivates diverse annotation pools and reporting group-wise agreement.
proof: Empirical: controlled comparisons of annotator groups show different label proportions on identical items.
consequence: Raises questions about whose judgments datasets encode.

title: Stratified Sampling Preserves Group Proportions
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Stratified sampling draws examples separately from each subgroup in proportion to its population share, keeping subgroup representation stable.
short: Sample each subgroup in proportion to its size.
detail: It reduces variance for subgroup estimates compared with simple random sampling.
proof: Fixing per-stratum counts removes sampling variability in group sizes.
consequence: Important for evaluating performance across demographic groups.

title: Class Imbalance Distorts Average Accuracy
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: With strongly imbalanced classes, a classifier can achieve high accuracy by ignoring the minority class entirely.
short: Overall accuracy can hide minority failures.
detail: Precision, recall and balanced accuracy reveal the problem.
proof: Always predicting the majority class is correct on exactly its population share.
consequence: Requires imbalance-aware metrics and evaluation.

title: Duplicate Examples Inflate Validation Scores
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Duplicates shared between training and validation splits make the validation set measure memorization instead of generalization.
short: Repeated examples leak answers across splits.
detail: Deduplication should happen before splitting.
proof: A memorized duplicate is predicted correctly without any generalization.
consequence: A common cause of irreproducible machine-learning results.

title: Near-Duplicate Leakage Across Split Boundaries
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Paraphrases or slight edits of a training example can leak into a test set even when exact deduplication is applied.
short: Near copies leak where exact copies do not.
detail: Fuzzy matching and embedding similarity help detect such leakage.
proof: Empirical: benchmark audits find high-similarity pairs across train and test splits.
consequence: Requires similarity-based as well as exact contamination checks.

title: Synthetic Data Can Amplify Bias Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, generating training data from a model can amplify biases present in the generator instead of correcting them.
short: Generated data can magnify existing skew.
detail: Filtering and balancing generated samples can mitigate the effect.
proof: Empirical: audits of synthetic datasets show increased skew in attribute distributions.
consequence: Synthetic augmentation needs bias monitoring.

title: Model Collapse from Generated Training Data Is Empirical
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, repeatedly training on generated data can cause distributions to lose tail information and accumulate errors, a phenomenon called model collapse.
short: Recursive synthetic training can erode diversity.
detail: Mixing real data and filtering generated samples slows the effect.
proof: Empirical: recursive training experiments show progressive loss of distribution tails.
consequence: Highlights the value of preserving authentic data.

title: Active Learning Queries Informative Examples
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Active learning selects which unlabeled examples to annotate, aiming to improve the model with fewer labels.
short: Ask for labels where they help most.
detail: The acquisition function trades informativeness against redundancy.
proof: Choose examples by an uncertainty or expected-progress criterion, label them and retrain.
consequence: Reduces annotation cost when labels are expensive.

title: Uncertainty Sampling Selects Ambiguous Inputs
subject: Machine Learning
statement: A common active-learning strategy queries examples whose predicted class is least confident or whose entropy is highest.
short: Label the points the model is most unsure about.
detail: Variance-based variants work for regression.
proof: High predictive entropy indicates disagreement among classes and often high information gain.
consequence: Simple and widely used, though it can select outliers.

title: MinHash Estimates Jaccard Similarity
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: MinHash represents a set by the minimum hash of its elements; the probability that two sets share a minimum equals their Jaccard similarity.
short: Hash minima estimate set overlap.
detail: Banding hash values makes near-duplicate retrieval efficient.
proof: The minimum over a union is equally likely to come from the intersection or either difference.
consequence: A standard tool for large-scale deduplication.

title: Group DRO Minimizes Worst-Group Risk
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Group distributionally robust optimization minimizes the highest loss among predefined groups rather than the average loss.
short: Train for the worst-performing subgroup.
detail: It improves worst-group accuracy when groups are known at training time.
proof: The minimax objective directly penalizes the group with highest empirical loss.
consequence: A baseline for robust and fair classification.

title: Equalized Odds Can Conflict with Calibration
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Except in special cases, a nonconstant predictor cannot simultaneously satisfy equalized odds across groups and be calibrated within each group when base rates differ.
short: Two reasonable fairness goals can be incompatible.
detail: Choosing a fairness criterion therefore requires value judgments.
proof: Conditioning on the same score distribution across groups while calibrating each group forces equal positive rates and hence equal base rates.
consequence: Shows why fairness definitions must be chosen explicitly.

title: Fairness through Awareness Uses Pairwise Metrics
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Fairness through awareness requires that similar individuals receive similar outcomes, with similarity defined by a task-appropriate metric.
short: Similar people should get similar decisions.
detail: It licenses using protected attributes when they help define appropriate similarity.
proof: The Lipschitz-style condition formalizes the requirement that outcomes vary continuously with task-relevant similarity.
consequence: Contrasts with fairness through unawareness.

title: Magnitude Pruning Removes Small Weights
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Magnitude pruning iteratively removes weights with smallest absolute value and usually retrains the remaining network.
short: Drop the smallest weights and retrain.
detail: Iterative pruning with gradual sparsity schedules works better than one-shot pruning.
proof: Small-magnitude weights contribute little to the current output; retraining compensates for the removed ones.
consequence: A simple and widely used compression technique.

title: Structured Pruning Removes Whole Units
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Structured pruning removes entire channels, heads or layers instead of individual weights, producing hardware-friendly sparse models.
short: Prune whole units rather than single connections.
detail: It sacrifices some flexibility for regular compute savings.
proof: Deleting a full structured block reduces the dimensions of matrix operations.
consequence: Delivers actual latency gains on standard hardware.

title: Post-Training Quantization Lowers Weight Precision
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Post-training quantization converts trained weights and sometimes activations to lower-precision integers without retraining.
short: Round trained weights to fewer bits.
detail: Calibration data sets the scale for activation quantization.
proof: A scale factor maps a real range onto a finite integer grid; rounding approximates each weight.
consequence: Shrinks memory and accelerates inference.

title: Quantization-Aware Training Simulates Low Precision
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Quantization-aware training inserts fake-quantization operations during training so the network adapts to finite precision before deployment.
short: Train with quantization simulated in the loop.
detail: Straight-through estimators approximate gradients through rounding.
proof: Forward passes apply quantization noise while backward passes use a surrogate gradient, letting weights adapt.
consequence: Recovers accuracy lost to naive post-training quantization.

title: INT8 Weights Quarter Model Memory
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Storing weights in 8 bits instead of 32 bits reduces the memory needed for weights by a factor of four.
short: Eight-bit weights take one quarter the space.
detail: Additional metadata such as scales adds a small overhead.
proof: Memory is bits per parameter times the number of parameters; the ratio is 32 divided by 8.
consequence: Enables larger models on memory-limited devices.

title: Knowledge Distillation Transfers Soft Targets
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Distillation trains a student to match a teacher's soft output probabilities in addition to the true labels.
short: Learn from the teacher's full distribution.
detail: Soft targets carry information about similarity between classes.
proof: The KL term aligns the student distribution with the teacher's softened distribution.
consequence: Often yields better compact models than training on hard labels alone.

title: Distillation Temperature Controls Target Softness
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Dividing logits by a temperature above one before softmax flattens the teacher distribution and exposes more information about non-top classes.
short: Higher temperature makes soft targets softer.
detail: Too much smoothing discards useful confidence information.
proof: Increasing temperature reduces logit gaps inside the softmax exponent, equalizing probabilities.
consequence: Temperature is a key distillation hyperparameter.

title: Dark Knowledge Lives in Relative Logit Gaps
subject: Neural Networks
statement: The usefulness of soft targets comes from the relative probabilities assigned to non-target classes, which reveal the teacher's similarity structure.
short: Class similarities hide in the small probabilities.
detail: Hard labels discard these relationships entirely.
proof: With a shared temperature the log ratio of softened probabilities equals the logit difference divided by temperature.
consequence: Explains why distillation can beat label-only training.

title: Self-Distillation Improves Students Empirically
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Empirically, a model can act as its own teacher across training stages or augmented views, improving generalization without an external teacher.
short: A model can teach a later copy of itself.
detail: Born-again networks and noisy-student training are related ideas.
proof: Empirical: self-distillation runs report lower test error than matched supervised baselines.
consequence: Provides regularization without a separate teacher.

title: Low-Rank Factorization Compresses Weight Matrices
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Approximating a large weight matrix by two thin matrices reduces parameters when the matrix has low effective rank.
latex: W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\approx UV,\ U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\ r\ll\min(m,n)
short: Factorize a big matrix into two thin ones.
detail: Truncated SVD gives the optimal low-rank approximation in Frobenius norm.
proof: The Eckart-Young theorem states truncated SVD minimizes reconstruction error for a fixed rank.
consequence: Reduces storage and compute for redundant layers.

title: LoRA Freezes Base Weights
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Low-rank adaptation freezes pretrained weights and trains only small rank-decomposition matrices added to selected linear layers.
short: Fine-tune tiny low-rank updates only.
detail: The base model can be shared across many adapted tasks.
proof: Restricting updates to a low-rank subspace dramatically reduces trainable parameters while retaining expressive task shifts.
consequence: Makes adaptation of large models affordable.

title: Adapter Layers Add Small Trainable Modules
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Adapters insert small bottleneck modules between frozen pretrained layers and train only those modules for a new task.
short: Slot tiny trainable blocks into a frozen model.
detail: Different tasks can keep separate adapter weights.
proof: The down-projection limits the number of trainable parameters, while the residual path preserves the base computation.
consequence: Enables parameter-efficient multitask serving.

title: Mixture of Experts Routes Tokens to Specialists
subject: Neural Networks
statement: A mixture-of-experts layer uses a router to send each token to a small subset of expert feed-forward networks.
short: Each token is handled by a few expert subnetworks.
detail: Load-balancing losses prevent all tokens from choosing the same experts.
proof: A router produces scores; top-k gating selects experts and weights their outputs.
consequence: Scales model capacity without proportional per-token compute.

title: Sparse MoE Reduces Per-Token Compute
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Sparse mixture-of-experts models grow total parameter count while activating only a fraction of experts per token, lowering compute per token.
short: Big model, small active subset per token.
detail: Memory cost rises even when compute stays moderate.
proof: Top-k routing evaluates only k of E experts for each token.
consequence: A major route to large-capacity efficient models.

title: KV Cache Memory Grows with Sequence Length
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Autoregressive decoding stores key and value tensors for previous tokens, so cache memory grows linearly with context length and number of layers.
short: Long contexts cost memory during generation.
detail: Grouped-query attention reduces the number of stored key-value heads.
proof: Each previous token contributes one key-value pair per layer and head.
consequence: Explains practical context-length limits.

title: FlashAttention Avoids Materializing Full Attention
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles, avoiding storage of the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory.
short: Tiled exact attention saves memory traffic.
detail: It uses an online softmax to combine tiles correctly.
proof: Streaming the softmax normalization across tiles yields the same result as full attention with far fewer memory writes.
consequence: Speeds up long-context training and inference.

title: Gradient Checkpointing Trades Compute for Memory
subject: Optimization
statement: Gradient checkpointing stores only a subset of activations and recomputes the rest during backpropagation.
short: Recompute activations instead of storing them.
detail: It enables training deeper models within a fixed memory budget.
proof: Discarded activations are recomputed from the nearest saved checkpoint during the backward pass.
consequence: Exchanges extra computation for a large memory saving.

title: Mixed Precision Uses Low-Precision Compute
subject: Optimization
statement: Mixed-precision training performs matrix multiplications in half precision while keeping master weights and accumulation in higher precision.
short: Fast half-precision math, stable high-precision updates.
detail: Loss scaling prevents small gradients from underflowing in half precision.
proof: Reduced precision accelerates tensor-core arithmetic, while high-precision accumulation preserves update accuracy.
consequence: Substantially speeds up large-model training.

title: Sparse Attention Limits Pairwise Connections
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Sparse attention restricts each token to attend to a chosen subset of positions, reducing cost below the full quadratic pairing.
short: Attend to a few positions instead of all.
detail: Patterns include local windows, strided views and learned routing.
proof: Each query processes only k keys, so the number of pairwise scores is n times k.
consequence: Makes long sequences computationally tractable.

title: Sliding-Window Attention Bounds Context Cost
subject: Neural Networks
statement: Sliding-window attention lets each token attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens, making cost linear in sequence length.
short: Look only at a fixed recent window.
detail: Stacked layers widen the effective receptive field across depth.
proof: The attention matrix has O(nw) nonzero entries instead of O(n^2).
consequence: A simple scalable long-context approximation.

title: Speculative Decoding Uses a Draft Model
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in parallel, accepting only tokens consistent with the large model's distribution.
short: Draft many tokens, verify them in one pass.
detail: The acceptance rule preserves the large model's output distribution.
proof: Rejection sampling with the ratio of target to draft probabilities yields exact samples from the target distribution.
consequence: Speeds up inference without changing outputs.

title: Early Exit Reduces Average Inference Depth
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Early-exit models attach classifiers to intermediate layers and stop processing once a confidence threshold is reached.
short: Stop when an intermediate layer is confident.
detail: Easy examples finish sooner than hard ones.
proof: A confidence rule permits prediction without running deeper layers; empirical studies show many examples exit early.
consequence: Lowers average latency for mixed-difficulty traffic.

title: Distillation Can Transfer Teacher Biases Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, a student trained on a teacher's soft targets can inherit the teacher's spurious associations and biases.
short: Students can learn a teacher's flaws too.
detail: Filtering teacher outputs or adding fairness constraints can reduce transfer.
proof: Empirical: students reproduce systematic errors present in teacher predictions on biased validation slices.
consequence: Distillation requires auditing the teacher, not only accuracy.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Conditions on Documents
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: RAG first retrieves relevant documents from an external corpus and then generates an answer conditioned on the query and retrieved text.
short: Fetch evidence, then write the answer.
detail: Knowledge can be updated by changing the corpus rather than the weights.
proof: The retrieved documents act as additional conditioning context for the generator.
consequence: Reduces reliance on parametric memorization.

title: Dense Retrieval Ranks by Embedding Similarity
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Dense retrieval encodes queries and documents into vectors and ranks documents by a similarity such as the dot product or cosine.
short: Embed query and documents, then rank by similarity.
detail: Dual-encoder training uses positive and negative document pairs.
proof: A learned encoder maps text to a shared space where relevant pairs have high inner product.
consequence: Enables semantic search beyond exact keyword matching.

title: BM25 Combines Term Frequency and IDF
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: BM25 ranks documents by saturating term frequency weighted by inverse document frequency and normalized by document length.
short: A classic lexical ranking function.
detail: It remains a strong baseline for sparse retrieval.
proof: The formula damps repeated terms and downweights common terms while adjusting for length.
consequence: Often combined with dense retrieval for hybrid search.

title: Vector Indexes Approximate Nearest Neighbour Search
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Approximate nearest neighbour indexes trade exactness for speed when searching embeddings at large scale.
short: Find likely nearest vectors quickly.
detail: Graph-based and partition-based indexes are common families.
proof: Index structures prune the candidate set, reducing comparisons at the cost of occasional misses.
consequence: Makes dense retrieval practical for millions of documents.

title: Document Chunking Affects Retrieval Quality Empirically
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirically, the size and overlap of document chunks influence RAG quality because chunks determine what evidence can be retrieved intact.
short: How you cut documents changes what you can find.
detail: Small chunks lose context; large chunks dilute relevance.
proof: Empirical: RAG evaluations vary chunk size and overlap and observe material score changes.
consequence: Chunking is a key indexing design choice.

title: RAG Reduces Hallucination but Does Not Eliminate It Empirically
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirically, retrieval augmentation lowers unsupported claims but generators can still produce statements not entailed by retrieved passages.
short: Evidence helps, but the model can still make things up.
detail: Faithfulness checks and citation verification remain necessary.
proof: Empirical: human and automatic audits find residual unsupported claims in RAG outputs.
consequence: Retrieval is not a complete solution to hallucination.

title: Retrieval Quality Bottlenecks RAG Empirically
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirically, RAG answer quality is often limited more by whether the correct passage is retrieved than by the generator's writing ability.
short: You cannot cite evidence you did not find.
detail: Improving retrievers can yield larger gains than swapping generators.
proof: Empirical: accuracy on queries with the gold passage present far exceeds accuracy when it is absent.
consequence: Prioritize retriever evaluation in RAG systems.

title: Re-Ranking Improves Retrieved Context Precision
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: A re-ranker scores a shortlist of retrieved documents with a more expensive cross-encoder and reorders them before generation.
short: Score a shortlist more carefully.
detail: Cross-encoders model query-document interaction but are too slow for full corpora.
proof: Joint encoding of query and document gives a more accurate relevance score than independent embeddings.
consequence: Raises the quality of context passed to the generator.

title: Query Reformulation Expands Retrieval Recall
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Rewriting or expanding a query before retrieval can recover documents missed by the original wording.
short: Rephrase the question to find more evidence.
detail: Multi-query and step-back prompting are common variants.
proof: Alternative phrasings match different lexical and semantic neighborhoods of the corpus.
consequence: Improves recall in complex question answering.

title: Hallucination Is Fluent Unsupported Generation
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Hallucination is the generation of content that is fluent and plausible but unsupported by the input or by reliable knowledge.
short: Confident words without supporting evidence.
detail: It differs from ordinary error because the output is presented as fact.
proof: The definition is operationalized by checking generations against sources or known facts.
consequence: A central reliability problem for language models.

title: Tool Use via Function Calling
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Tool use lets a language model emit structured calls to external functions and incorporate their returned results into its answer.
short: Models can call code, search and APIs.
detail: Schemas constrain argument types and reduce malformed calls.
proof: The model is trained or prompted to produce tool invocations, whose outputs are inserted back into the context.
consequence: Extends models beyond their parametric knowledge.

title: ReAct Interleaves Reasoning and Tool Actions
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: ReAct prompts a model to alternate short reasoning traces with environment actions and observations before producing an answer.
short: Think, act, observe, repeat.
detail: Observations ground later reasoning in external results.
proof: Empirical: interleaving improves performance on knowledge and decision tasks compared with reasoning or acting alone.
consequence: A widely used agent interaction pattern.

title: Reflexion Revises Plans from Verbal Feedback
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Reflexion stores verbal self-feedback from failed attempts in memory and uses it to revise the next attempt.
short: Learn from mistakes in natural-language memory.
detail: It is a test-time adaptation loop without weight updates.
proof: Empirical: verbal feedback persisted across trials improves success rates on sequential tasks.
consequence: Shows how memory can substitute for gradient learning.

title: Toolformer Learns API Calls from Text Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Toolformer self-supervises insertion of API calls into text by keeping only calls whose results improve next-token prediction, an empirical method.
short: Learn which tool calls help predict text.
detail: The filtering step removes calls that degrade the language-modeling objective.
proof: Empirical: filtered self-labeled calls teach the model to invoke calculators and search tools usefully.
consequence: Demonstrates self-supervised tool acquisition.

title: Agent Error Compounds Across Long Horizons Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, multi-step agents accumulate mistakes because each erroneous action changes the state for all later steps.
short: Small step errors multiply over long tasks.
detail: Checks, backtracking and verification break the chain of compounding.
proof: Success requires every critical step to be correct, so independent per-step success probabilities multiply.
consequence: Explains poor scaling of agents to long horizons.

title: External Memory Extends Agent Context
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: An agent can store observations and plans in an external memory and retrieve them later, avoiding limits on the model context window.
short: Keep notes outside the context window.
detail: Memory may be a vector store, a scratchpad or a structured database.
proof: Writing and retrieving decouples stored information from a single prompt.
consequence: Enables longer-running and more consistent agent behavior.

title: Guardrails Filter Unsafe Agent Actions
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Guardrails are external checks that block or revise model outputs or actions that violate specified rules.
short: Put a safety layer around the model.
detail: They can inspect tool arguments, outputs and environment effects.
proof: A rule checker evaluates proposed actions before execution and vetoes disallowed ones.
consequence: Provides defense in depth beyond model training.

title: Tool Documentation Improves Call Accuracy Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, clear tool descriptions and argument schemas increase the rate of correct tool selection and invocation.
short: Good API docs help models call tools.
detail: Ambiguous overlapping descriptions cause selection errors.
proof: Empirical: ablations of tool descriptions change call accuracy on tool-use benchmarks.
consequence: Tool interfaces should be designed for models as well as humans.

title: Agent Benchmarks Measure Task Success Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Agent benchmarks evaluate systems by the fraction of simulated software or web tasks completed, using automated checks of final state.
short: Judge agents by completed tasks, not prose.
detail: SWE-bench and WebArena are prominent examples of this evaluation style.
proof: Each task supplies an environment and tests that verify the final state.
consequence: Captures capabilities that static question answering misses.

title: CLIP Aligns Image and Text Embeddings Empirically
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Empirically, contrastive image-text pretraining places matching images and captions near each other in a shared embedding space, enabling zero-shot classification.
short: Learn a shared space for pictures and words.
detail: Zero-shot classification compares an image to text prompts for each class.
proof: Empirical: trained encoders rank the correct caption above mismatched ones and make text-prompted classification work.
consequence: A foundation for modern vision-language systems.

title: Contrastive Pretraining Uses In-Batch Negatives
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Contrastive pretraining treats other paired examples in the same batch as negative pairs and maximizes similarity for the matched pairs.
short: Matched pairs attract, other batch pairs repel.
detail: Larger batches supply more negatives but require more memory.
proof: TheInfoNCE-style objective is cross-entropy over which batch item is the correct match.
consequence: Efficiently learns aligned multimodal representations.

title: Vision-Language Projectors Bridge Encoders
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Vision-language models map image encoder outputs into the language model token space with a learned projector or adapter.
short: Translate image features into token embeddings.
detail: The projector is often a small linear map or multilayer perceptron.
proof: Projected visual features share dimensionality with word embeddings and can be fed to the language backbone.
consequence: Allows reuse of pretrained unimodal encoders.

title: Cross-Attention Conditions Text on Image Features
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: In encoder-decoder vision-language models, decoder tokens attend to image features through cross-attention to produce grounded text.
short: Text generation can attend to picture features.
detail: This is the standard mechanism in captioning and visual question answering.
proof: Keys and values come from image features while queries come from the text decoder.
consequence: Enables generation that depends on visual content.

title: Image Captioning Uses Encoder-Decoder Models
subject: Computer Vision
statement: Image captioning encodes a picture into features and decodes them into a natural-language description, often with attention.
short: Turn an image into a sentence.
detail: Training maximizes likelihood of reference captions.
proof: The encoder supplies a conditional context for an autoregressive language decoder.
consequence: A canonical multimodal generation task.

title: Visual Question Answering Requires Grounding
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Visual question answering needs both language understanding and grounding of entities in the image, so language priors alone are insufficient.
short: Answering about an image needs the image.
detail: Models can exploit dataset biases and answer without looking.
proof: Empirical ablations show accuracy drops when visual input is replaced by a prior-only baseline.
consequence: Motivates explicit grounding and bias-resistant benchmarks.

title: Modality Gap Separates Image and Text Spaces
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Empirically, image and text embeddings from contrastive models occupy distinct cones even after alignment, leaving a modality gap.
short: The two modalities live in different regions.
detail: The gap can be measured as the displacement between embedding centroids.
proof: Empirical: mean image and text embeddings are separated by a consistent vector across layers and datasets.
consequence: Affects retrieval and zero-shot transfer.

title: Modality Imbalance Causes Lazy Learning Empirically
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Empirically, when one modality is more predictive than another, multimodal models may rely mostly on the strong modality and underuse the weak one.
short: A dominant modality can make the other lazy.
detail: Modality-specific dropout and weighting can rebalance learning.
proof: Empirical: ablating the strong modality causes larger performance drops than ablating the weak one.
consequence: A common failure mode in multimodal training.

title: Late Fusion Combines Modality Scores
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Late fusion trains separate unimodal models and combines their predictions or scores at the end.
short: Predict per modality, then combine.
detail: It handles missing modalities easily but misses cross-modal interactions.
proof: Each modality produces a score; a weighted combination yields a joint decision.
consequence: A robust baseline for multimodal tasks.

title: Early Fusion Concatenates Modality Features
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Early fusion concatenates features from different modalities before passing them to a joint model.
short: Merge features before making predictions.
detail: It allows interactions but requires aligned inputs.
proof: Feature concatenation forms a single joint representation consumed by downstream layers.
consequence: Enables learned cross-modal interactions.

title: Spectrograms Represent Time-Frequency Content
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: A spectrogram shows how the frequency content of an audio signal changes over time, usually from a short-time Fourier transform.
short: A picture of sound frequencies over time.
detail: Log-mel spectrograms are common inputs to audio models.
proof: Windowed Fourier transforms produce frequency magnitudes per time frame.
consequence: Allows image-style models to process audio.

title: Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients Compress Speech
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: MFCCs summarize the spectral envelope on a mel scale using a cosine transform of log filter-bank energies.
short: Compact features that mimic human hearing.
detail: They were a standard front end for speech recognition before learned features.
proof: The discrete cosine transform decorrelates log mel energies into a small cepstral vector.
consequence: A classic speech-feature representation.

title: Wav2Vec Learns Speech Representations Empirically
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Wav2Vec learns speech representations by contrastive self-supervision over masked audio latents and negative samples, an empirical method.
short: Learn audio features from raw waveform structure.
detail: Fine-tuning on transcripts yields strong speech recognition with limited labeled data.
proof: Empirical: contrastive pretraining on unlabeled audio improves downstream recognition accuracy.
consequence: Shows self-supervision works for speech.

title: CTC Loss Aligns Unsegmented Speech to Text
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Connectionist temporal classification sums probability over all monotonic frame-to-label alignments, including blanks, so transcription needs no pre-segmentation.
short: Marginalize over unknown alignments.
detail: The blank symbol permits repeated labels and silence.
proof: Forward-backward over the lattice of alignments computes the total probability of collapsing to the target sequence.
consequence: A standard loss for sequence transcription.

title: Whisper Trains on Weakly Supervised Transcripts Empirically
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Empirically, large-scale weakly supervised transcription training yields a speech model that generalizes across languages and tasks.
short: Massive noisy transcripts produce robust speech models.
detail: Task prompts let one model perform transcription and translation.
proof: Empirical: training on diverse web-scale audio-text pairs improves robustness on held-out speech benchmarks.
consequence: Highlights the value of scale and diversity in audio data.

title: Text-to-Speech Uses Acoustic Models and Vocoders
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Text-to-speech systems map text to an acoustic representation such as a mel spectrogram and then synthesize a waveform with a vocoder.
short: Predict a spectrogram, then turn it into audio.
detail: Modern systems may also generate audio tokens directly.
proof: The acoustic model produces time-frequency features and the vocoder inverts them into samples.
consequence: Separates linguistic content from waveform synthesis.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models Map Pixels to Actions
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Vision-language-action models condition a policy on images and language instructions to output robot actions.
short: One model turns images and words into robot motions.
detail: They are typically fine-tuned from vision-language backbones on robot trajectories.
proof: The observation and instruction are encoded jointly and decoded as an action sequence.
consequence: Shows transfer of web-scale representations to embodied control.

title: Cross-Modal Retrieval Uses Shared Embeddings
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Cross-modal retrieval maps queries and candidate items from different modalities into a shared space and ranks by embedding similarity.
short: Search images with text using one shared space.
detail: The same machinery supports text-to-image and image-to-text search.
proof: Joint training aligns encoders so that paired items have high similarity.
consequence: Underpins multilingual and multimodal search interfaces.

title: Typographic Attacks Mislead Vision-Language Models Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, placing misleading text inside an image can flip a vision-language model's classification toward the written word.
short: Words printed in an image can fool the model.
detail: This reveals heavy reliance on linguistic features in visual encoders.
proof: Empirical: adding a text label to an object image changes predicted class in controlled experiments.
consequence: A concrete robustness failure of multimodal systems.

title: Partially Observable MDP Has Hidden State
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: A partially observable Markov decision process extends an MDP by giving the agent observations generated from a hidden state rather than the state itself.
short: The agent sees observations, not the true state.
detail: Policies may keep belief states or recurrent memory.
proof: The transition and observation models define a belief update over hidden states.
consequence: Models realistic robotics and planning under uncertainty.

title: Model Predictive Control Replans Each Step
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Model predictive control solves a finite-horizon optimal-control problem at each step, applies the first action and replans with new observations.
short: Plan briefly, act once, then replan.
detail: Receding-horizon replanning corrects model errors.
proof: At each time a fresh optimization uses the current state estimate and discards the rest of the old plan.
consequence: A standard robust control strategy in robotics.

title: Imitation Learning Clones Expert Actions
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Behavioral cloning learns a policy by supervised regression from expert state-action demonstrations.
short: Learn to copy the expert's actions.
detail: It needs no reward function but depends on demonstration coverage.
proof: The expert action is treated as a supervised label for each demonstrated state.
consequence: A simple way to bootstrap policies from data.

title: Behavioral Cloning Suffers Covariate Shift
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Small cloning errors move the agent off the demonstration distribution, where further errors grow and compound.
short: One small mistake leads to unfamiliar states.
detail: This is why cloned policies can fail despite low held-out action error.
proof: A wrong action changes the next state, which may lie outside the support of demonstrations.
consequence: Motivates data aggregation and on-policy correction methods.

title: DAgger Aggregates Expert Corrections
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Dataset aggregation iteratively runs the current policy, asks an expert to label visited states and retrains on the growing dataset.
short: Collect expert corrections on the states the learner visits.
detail: This addresses the covariate shift of behavioral cloning.
proof: Adding expert labels for learner-induced states makes the training distribution match the deployment distribution.
consequence: Improves imitation stability in sequential tasks.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning Infers Rewards
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function under which observed expert behavior is near-optimal.
short: Infer what goal explains the demonstrations.
detail: The inferred reward can generalize to new situations.
proof: Optimality conditions link behavior to rewards, so demonstration likelihood can score candidate rewards.
consequence: Bases preferences on goals rather than copied actions.

title: Domain Randomization Aids Sim-to-Real Transfer Empirically
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Domain randomization varies simulator parameters widely during training so that real-world dynamics appear as one sample from the training distribution, an empirical technique.
short: Train on many simulated worlds to handle the real one.
detail: Randomized visuals and physics encourage robust policies.
proof: Empirical: policies trained with wide parameter variation transfer better to real robots than single-environment training.
consequence: Reduces the reality gap in robotics.

title: Offline RL Learns from Fixed Datasets
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed logged dataset without further interaction with the environment.
short: Learn from logged experience only.
detail: Extrapolation errors on unseen actions are the main challenge.
proof: The dataset replaces online rollouts as the source of transitions.
consequence: Makes RL applicable where exploration is costly or unsafe.

title: Conservative Q-Learning Penalizes OOD Actions
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Conservative Q-learning adds a penalty that lowers Q-values for actions not present in the offline dataset, reducing extrapolation error.
short: Keep Q-values low for unfamiliar actions.
detail: This discourages the policy from exploiting erroneous high estimates.
proof: The penalty subtracts expected Q on dataset actions from a log-sum-exp over all actions.
consequence: A standard baseline for offline RL.

title: Safety Shields Filter Unsafe Actions
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: A safety shield monitors proposed actions and replaces those that violate a formal safety specification with safe alternatives.
short: A runtime filter blocks dangerous actions.
detail: Shields can be synthesized from temporal-logic constraints.
proof: The checker evaluates the action against the specification before execution.
consequence: Gives formal safety guarantees at runtime.

title: Occupancy Grids Represent Free Space
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: An occupancy grid discretizes the environment into cells marked free, occupied or unknown for robot planning.
short: A map of which cells are blocked.
detail: Sensor readings update cell probabilities over time.
proof: Discretizing space and fusing measurements yields a per-cell occupancy estimate.
consequence: A basic representation for mobile-robot navigation.

title: Structural Causal Model Encodes Interventions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: A structural causal model consists of exogenous noise variables and structural equations that define each variable as a function of its parents and noise.
short: Variables are generated by explicit mechanisms.
detail: An intervention replaces one structural equation with a fixed value.
proof: The equations define the observational distribution and, after replacement, interventional distributions.
consequence: Provides a formal language for causality.

title: do-Calculus Identifies Interventional Distributions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Do-calculus gives three rules for transforming probabilities with interventions into expressions involving only observational distributions when graphical conditions hold.
short: Rewrite interventions as observations when possible.
detail: Identification fails when confounding cannot be blocked.
proof: The rules follow from the invariance of mechanisms under interventions in a causal DAG.
consequence: Foundation of causal inference from observational data.

title: Backdoor Criterion Blocks Spurious Paths
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: The backdoor criterion identifies a set of covariates whose adjustment removes confounding between treatment and outcome in a causal graph.
short: Adjust for variables that close backdoor paths.
detail: Adjusting for colliders can instead create bias.
proof: Conditioning on a valid backdoor set blocks every noncausal path from treatment to outcome.
consequence: Justifies covariate adjustment in observational studies.

title: Frontdoor Criterion Identifies Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: The frontdoor criterion identifies a causal effect through an observed mediator even when treatment and outcome share unobserved confounding.
short: Use a mediator to bypass hidden confounding.
detail: It requires the mediator to intercept all causal paths and be unconfounded with the outcome given treatment.
proof: The identification formula chains the treatment-to-mediator and mediator-to-outcome effects.
consequence: Enables identification in some otherwise intractable settings.

title: Instrumental Variables Handle Unobserved Confounding
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: An instrumental variable affects the outcome only through the treatment, allowing identification despite unobserved treatment-outcome confounding.
short: Use an external nudge to isolate causal effect.
detail: Validity requires relevance, independence and exclusion restrictions.
proof: The instrument shifts treatment without directly changing the outcome, so its association with the outcome scales with the causal effect.
consequence: A central tool in econometrics and causal ML.

title: Difference-in-Differences Removes Time-Invariant Bias
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Difference-in-differences estimates a treatment effect by comparing pre-to-post changes in treated and untreated groups.
short: Compare changes, not just levels.
detail: It relies on parallel trends in the absence of treatment.
proof: Time-invariant group differences cancel in the double difference.
consequence: Widely used for policy and observational effect estimation.

title: Propensity Score Matching Balances Covariates
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Propensity score matching pairs treated and control units with similar probabilities of treatment given covariates to reduce confounding.
short: Match people with similar treatment chances.
detail: Balance diagnostics check whether matching succeeded.
proof: Conditional on the propensity score, treatment is independent of covariates under ignorability.
consequence: A common observational causal estimator.

title: Double Machine Learning Debiases Treatment Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Double machine learning uses cross-fitted nuisance estimates and orthogonal scores so that regularization errors do not bias the treatment-effect estimate.
short: Cross-fit nuisances to remove first-order bias.
detail: Neyman orthogonality makes the estimator robust to slow nuisance learning.
proof: Cross-fitting independentizes nuisance estimates from the evaluation sample and orthogonality cancels first-order errors.
consequence: Brings flexible ML into valid causal inference.

title: Causal Forests Estimate Heterogeneous Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Causal forests use tree ensembles with honest splitting to estimate how treatment effects vary across covariates.
short: Trees that estimate local treatment effects.
detail: Honest splitting uses separate data for tree structure and effect estimation.
proof: Local randomized or residualized comparisons are averaged over trees to produce conditional effect estimates.
consequence: Supports personalized treatment-effect estimation.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Seeks Stable Predictors
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Invariant risk minimization aims to learn representations whose optimal classifier is the same across training environments, encouraging out-of-distribution generalization.
short: Seek features that work the same in every environment.
detail: The penalty encourages the invariance of the optimal linear predictor.
proof: Requiring a shared optimal classifier across environments discourages reliance on environment-specific correlations.
consequence: A theoretical approach to causal feature learning.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Can Fail Empirically
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Empirically, invariant risk minimization can fail on nonlinear or insufficiently varied environments, sometimes learning degenerate invariant solutions.
short: Invariance penalties do not always deliver robustness.
detail: Careful environment design and diagnostics matter.
proof: Empirical: constructed nonlinear tasks show IRM converging to trivial constant classifiers.
consequence: Highlights gaps between invariance theory and practice.

title: Truncated Factorization Gives Interventional Distributions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: In a causal Bayesian network, the distribution after intervening on a set of variables factors with the structural equations for the intervened variables replaced by point masses.
latex: P(y\mid do(x))=\prod_{i\notin X}P(x_i\mid x_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})\ \mathbf{1}[x_i=\hat{x}_i\ \mathrm{for}\ i\in X]
short: Cut incoming edges for intervened nodes.
detail: This is the truncated factorization formula.
proof: The intervention removes the parents of each manipulated variable, so those factors vanish from the joint.
consequence: Connects graph structure to intervention calculations.

title: Counterfactual Fairness Requires a Causal Model
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Counterfactual fairness requires a decision to be unchanged in a counterfactual world where only the protected attribute is altered, which needs a causal model to define.
short: Fairness can be defined by counterfactual invariance.
detail: Without causal assumptions the counterfactual is not identifiable.
proof: Changing a protected attribute while holding other variables fixed requires specifying which descendants change.
consequence: Makes causal assumptions explicit in fairness analysis.

title: Collider Conditioning Can Reverse Associations
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Conditioning on a common effect of two variables can create a spurious association between them, potentially reversing the sign of an estimated effect.
latex: X\perp Y,\ \mathrm{but}\ X\not\perp Y\mid C,\ C\leftarrow X,\ C\leftarrow Y
short: Selecting on a common effect creates false dependence.
detail: This is Berkson's paradox or collider bias.
proof: Conditioning on a collider opens a path between its parents in the graphical criterion.
consequence: Warns against indiscriminate covariate adjustment.

title: Federated Averaging Aggregates Local Updates
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Federated averaging trains locally on each client for several steps and averages the resulting model updates on a server.
short: Train locally, average globally.
detail: Weighting by client sample size is the standard aggregation rule.
proof: Local SGD steps approximate a global step; averaging combines the clients' estimates.
consequence: The foundational algorithm of federated learning.

title: Federated Rounds Dominate Communication Cost
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: In federated learning the bottleneck is often the repeated exchange of model updates between server and clients, not local computation.
short: Sending models costs more than training locally.
detail: Compression and fewer local steps trade accuracy for less communication.
proof: Each round transmits a full model to selected clients and back, which dominates when models are large.
consequence: Drives research on communication-efficient federated algorithms.

title: Non-IID Clients Slow Federated Convergence Empirically
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Empirically, heterogeneous client data distributions make local updates diverge and slow or destabilize federated convergence.
short: Different clients pull the model in different directions.
detail: Personalization and proximal terms mitigate client drift.
